title: Grief Is Strange: You Can Laugh at Breakfast and Break Down in the Grocery Store
paragraphs: Grief Is Strange: You Can Laugh at Breakfast and Break Down in the Grocery Store
If you have ever wondered how you could worship God in the morning and cry beside a grocery cart that afternoon, there is something Jesus did beside a grave that you desperately need to see.
You were fine five minutes ago.
That is the part nobody warns you about.
You woke up. You made coffee. Maybe you even laughed at something on your phone. For a few precious minutes, life almost felt normal again.
Then you went to the grocery store.
You weren't looking for a memory.
You were looking for bread.
Milk.
Coffee.
Something for dinner.
And then you saw it.
Their favorite cereal.
The brand of tea they always bought.
A jar of sauce they insisted was better than every other jar on the shelf.
Maybe a song started playing overhead.
Maybe somebody walked past wearing the same perfume.
Maybe you heard a laugh that sounded almost—almost—like theirs.
And suddenly you weren't standing in aisle seven anymore.
You were standing in the ruins of a life that used to include someone who is no longer there.
Your throat tightened.
Your chest hurt.
Your eyes filled.
You stared at a grocery shelf while strangers pushed carts around you, completely unaware that your whole world had just collapsed again between the canned vegetables and the breakfast cereal.
And perhaps the worst part came afterward.
You felt guilty.
Why am I still doing this?
Shouldn't I be stronger by now?
I thought I was healing.
I was laughing this morning.
Why am I crying again?
And if you are a Christian, another question can creep into the darkness.
Does this mean my faith is weak?
Please stay here for a moment.
Because there is a scene in Scripture that refuses to let us treat tears as spiritual failure.
There is a grave.
There are grieving sisters.
There is a crowd trying to make sense of death.
And standing in the middle of it all is Jesus Christ.
John 11 tells us about Lazarus, the brother of Mary and Martha and a man Jesus loved.
Lazarus became sick.
Jesus knew.
Yet Jesus did not arrive before Lazarus died.
By the time Christ came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.
Martha went out to meet Him.
Mary eventually came too.
And when Mary reached Jesus, she fell at His feet with words that carry the sound of shattered expectation:
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.”
Then Mary wept.
The people around her wept.
And John tells us something extraordinary.
The Greek text of John 11:33 says:
“Ἰησοῦς οὖν ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὴν κλαίουσαν…”
Jesus saw her weeping.
Then comes language far stronger than a picture of a detached religious teacher calmly explaining why everything would eventually be okay.
“ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν.”
He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
Those Greek expressions matter.

John does not portray Jesus as emotionally untouched by the scene before Him. The language carries profound inner disturbance. Jesus enters the terrible reality surrounding death rather than standing at a safe emotional distance from it.
Then He asks:
“Where have ye laid him?”
They answer:
“Lord, come and see.”
And then comes one of the shortest verses in the Bible.
Two words in many English translations.
John 11:35.
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek is equally arresting:
“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.”
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
Jesus wept.
Read that again slowly.
Jesus knew what He was about to do.
Jesus knew Lazarus would not remain inside that tomb.
Jesus knew resurrection was only moments away.
And Jesus still wept.
That changes something.
Because we sometimes imagine that if we truly trust God, knowledge of the resurrection should somehow erase the agony of the grave.
But Jesus knew more about resurrection than anybody standing in Bethany that day.
And He cried.
He did not say, “Stop crying. Lazarus is coming back.”
He did not rebuke Mary for grieving.
He did not shame Martha because death had wounded her.
He did not stand outside human sorrow pretending that correct theology makes tears unnecessary.
He wept.
This is Christianity at the graveside.
Not hopelessness.
Not denial.
Hope with tears running down its face.
You can believe Jesus Christ is the resurrection and the life and still miss somebody so much that their empty chair hurts.
You can believe in heaven and still hate funerals.
You can know that death does not have the final word and still wish desperately that you could hear that person's voice one more time.
You can sing on Sunday and cry on Monday.
You can pray with confidence at 7:00 in the morning and feel your knees weaken when you find an old photograph at 3:17 in the afternoon.
You can laugh at breakfast...
and break down in the grocery store.
That does not automatically mean you have abandoned faith.
Sometimes it simply means you loved someone whose absence still has weight.
Grief is strange because grief does not ask permission before entering the room.
It does not check your calendar.
It does not care that today was supposed to be a good day.
It can hide inside birthdays.
Christmas songs.
Hospital corridors.
Empty bedrooms.
Old voicemail recordings.
A particular road.
A familiar smell.
A restaurant table.
A church pew.
A name appearing unexpectedly on an old document.
A phone number you cannot bring yourself to delete.
Sometimes grief screams.
Sometimes it whispers.
Sometimes it waits quietly for six months and then ambushes you because you reached for two coffee cups instead of one.
And there you are again.
Hurting.
Maybe embarrassed by how much you're hurting.
But Scripture never gives us a commandment saying, “Thou shalt finish grieving by Thursday.”
The Bible gives us lament.
David asks, “How long, O LORD?” in Psalm 13.
The Psalms contain cries, questions, anguish, loneliness and tears alongside praise, trust and worship.
Ecclesiastes says there is “a time to weep.”
Paul does not tell believers never to grieve. In 1 Thessalonians 4:13, he distinguishes Christian grief from grief without hope.
That distinction matters.
The Gospel does not turn Christians into people incapable of sorrow.
The Gospel gives sorrow somewhere to go.
Toward Christ.
Toward the One who stood outside Lazarus's tomb.
Toward the One who Himself would soon enter a tomb.
And this is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
Jesus did not merely come to Bethany to sympathize with people devastated by death.
He came to confront death.
He called:
“Lazarus, come forth.”
And the dead man came out.
But Lazarus's resurrection was a sign pointing beyond Lazarus.
Because another tomb was coming.
Another stone.
Another body wrapped for burial.
Another group of devastated followers convinced that everything had ended.
Except this time the dead Man inside the tomb would not need someone standing outside commanding Him to emerge.
Jesus Christ would rise.
The cross and empty tomb are God's declaration that death is an enemy—but it is a defeated enemy.
Sin brought ruin into God's good creation.
And all of us stand guilty before a holy God, needing far more than emotional comfort. We need reconciliation. We need forgiveness. We need redemption.
That is why Jesus did not merely come to make grieving people feel better.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
The Christian hope is therefore not vague optimism that somehow everything eventually works out.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
Our hope has an empty tomb.
Our hope has scars in His hands.
And because Christ lives, grief does not get the last sentence.
But notice something beautiful.
Jesus knew the last sentence before everybody else did...
and He still stopped to weep in the middle of the paragraph.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
In the middle.
You know what Christians are supposed to say.
“God is good.”
“He is with me.”
“I will see them again.”
“Jesus is faithful.”
And you believe those things.
But tonight you would also give almost anything to hear one more “hello.”
That longing does not surprise Christ.
Bring it to Him.
Not the polished version.
Not the Sunday-morning version.
Not the version cleaned up enough to make everybody else comfortable.
Bring Him the version that cries in parking lots.
Bring Him the anger you are afraid to admit.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the nights when everybody else has stopped checking on you because the funeral happened months ago.
Bring Him the anniversary nobody remembered.
Bring Him the clothes you cannot throw away.
Bring Him the photograph you still touch.
Bring Him the voicemail you keep replaying.
Bring Him the chair nobody sits in.
Bring Him the sentence you have been afraid to say:
“Jesus, I know You are good...
but this hurts.”
He already knows.
Christian lament is not pretending God is absent.
It is hurting honestly in His presence.
And maybe someone reading this has grief deeper than bereavement.
Perhaps you are grieving a marriage that ended.
A child who walked away.
A friendship that died without a funeral.
A pregnancy that ended before you ever got to hold the baby.
A future that disappeared after one doctor's appointment.
A parent who is still alive but no longer remembers your name.
A dream you prayed over for years that never happened.
A version of yourself you can never return to.
Not every grief has a cemetery.
Some graves are invisible.
Jesus sees those too.
And there is another kind of grief some people carry—the grief of what they themselves have done.
Regret.
Sin.
Years wasted.
People wounded.
Promises broken.
Secret compromises nobody knows about.
Perhaps you are not mourning somebody you lost.
Perhaps you are mourning who you became.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than comfort.
It becomes rescue.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem a sinner.
Repentance is not God demanding that you repair yourself before approaching Him. It is turning from sin and coming to Christ because you finally realize you cannot save yourself.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
The cross proves that sin matters terribly.
Grace says Christ was willing to bear what you could never bear and pay what you could never pay.
Your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your failure does not have to write the last chapter.
Your grief does not have to become your god.
Your grave does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if you are grieving today, perhaps healing will not look like never crying again.
Perhaps healing sometimes looks like realizing you can cry without drowning.
Perhaps tomorrow you will laugh.
And perhaps Thursday you will cry again.
Perhaps next month you will hear their favorite song and smile instead of collapse.
Perhaps six months later that same song will break you all over again.
Do not measure God's faithfulness by the predictability of your emotions.
Look instead at Christ.
The Christ who wept.
The Christ who suffered.
The Christ who died.
The Christ who rose.
The Christ who receives repentant sinners.
The Christ who promises resurrection.
The Christ who will not permit death to reign forever.
There is coming a day when what happened outside Lazarus's tomb will no longer be an isolated sign pointing toward something greater.
Revelation gives us the final horizon of Christian grief: God dwelling with His people, death defeated, mourning ended, tears wiped away.
Not because the people we loved were insignificant.
But because Christ has conquered the enemy that took them.
Until then...
sometimes we cry.
And sometimes we laugh.
Sometimes both happen on the same day.
That is not hypocrisy.
That is being human while waiting for resurrection.
So the next time grief finds you in a grocery store, do not immediately accuse yourself of failing God.
Maybe put your hand on the cart.
Breathe.
Let the tears come if they come.
And whisper the only prayer you can manage:
“Jesus, stay with me here.”
The One who wept outside a tomb is not frightened by your tears.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes two or three words are enough to tell another grieving believer, I am still here. I still believe. I am just hurting.
And if somebody's name entered your mind while you were reading this, send this article to them.
Not because an article can fix their grief.
It cannot.
Not necessarily for today.
For the grocery-store day.
For the birthday.
For Christmas.
For the anniversary.
For the unexpected song.
For the night grief returns without knocking.
And there is another way to stand with this ministry.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never could.
Scripture says giving is to come from a willing heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, do it freely, gratefully and with Christ—not Gospel Warrior—at the center.
Your sharing helps carry it farther.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments help create a community where hurting people discover they are not grieving alone.
If you are ready to become part of that support:
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the resurrection and the life.
No ministry can forgive your sins.
No writer can resurrect the dead.
Only Christ saves.
Only Christ conquered the grave.
Only Christ can take a sinner's scandal and write grace across the ending.
So repent where you need to repent.
Receive His grace.
Run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Cry when you need to cry.
Hold tightly to Scripture.
Stay near God's people.
And when grief surprises you again, remember Bethany.
Remember Mary crying at His feet.
Remember the crowd weeping.
Remember the stone.
Remember those astonishing Greek words:
“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.”
Jesus wept.
And then remember what happened next.
The tears were real.
But the tomb did not win.
Neither will yours.
One day, the Jesus who once wept beside a grave will make graves unnecessary forever.
